questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: repudiated
choices.B: continued to favor
choices.C: attributed
choices.D: reprimanded

questions.explanation:
The contrast establishes that although many manufacturers adopted synthetic materials, Tapiovaara continued using established woodworking methods. **“Continued to favor”** precisely conveys that he maintained a preference for those traditional practices.

A, “repudiated,” means rejected and would imply the opposite of what the examples show. C, “attributed,” means regarded something as being caused by or belonging to something else and does not fit the sentence grammatically or logically. D, “reprimanded,” means formally criticized or scolded, which has no sensible relationship to woodworking practices.

choiceExplanations.B: The contrast establishes that although many manufacturers adopted synthetic materials, Tapiovaara continued using established woodworking methods. **“Continued to favor”** precisely conveys that he maintained a preference for those traditional practices.

questions.passage: Architect Francis Kéré has received considerable attention for buildings that combine contemporary engineering with construction practices rooted in Burkina Faso, including the use of locally sourced materials and climate-responsive forms. Such synthesis is not unique to Kéré. In Bangladesh, architect Marina Tabassum has likewise incorporated regional materials and building traditions into projects shaped by contemporary architectural concerns.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Contemporary architects in different regions are integrating local building traditions with modern architectural approaches.
choices.B: Architects who use locally available materials generally complete projects more cheaply than architects who use imported materials.
choices.C: Kéré’s work has encouraged architects outside Burkina Faso to reproduce West African construction techniques.
choices.D: Contemporary architecture is gradually abandoning engineered materials in favor of traditional construction methods.

questions.explanation:
The passage first describes Kéré’s integration of contemporary engineering with regional building traditions and then presents Tabassum as another architect who similarly combines local practices with contemporary design. The broader point is therefore that **multiple contemporary architects are integrating traditional or regional building methods with modern architectural approaches**.

B is unsupported because the passage says nothing about comparative project costs. C wrongly proposes a causal relationship between Kéré’s work and other architects’ practices. D overstates the passage: the architects are combining traditional and contemporary approaches, not rejecting engineered or modern methods altogether.

choiceExplanations.A: The passage first describes Kéré’s integration of contemporary engineering with regional building traditions and then presents Tabassum as another architect who similarly combines local practices with contemporary design. The broader point is therefore that **multiple contemporary architects are integrating traditional or regional building methods with modern architectural approaches**.

questions.passage: Previous materials-science studies have reported that, across structurally diverse steel alloys, average grain size is negatively associated with yield strength. Yet M. Okafor and colleagues, in a 2022 investigation of specimens cut from a single nickel-steel alloy, detected no statistically significant association between the two variables. The researchers noted that earlier studies included alloys produced under widely varying compositions and heat treatments, whereas their own specimens had nearly identical compositions and had been annealed within a narrow temperature interval, producing only a limited range of grain sizes and strengths.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that restricting a study to one alloy proves that the previously observed relationship between grain size and yield strength does not exist
choices.B: To explain why a relationship detected across varied materials may not have appeared in a study whose samples exhibited relatively little variation
choices.C: To demonstrate that annealing temperature determines yield strength more strongly than grain size does in all nickel-steel alloys
choices.D: To establish that correlations between grain size and yield strength depend primarily on whether an alloy contains nickel

questions.explanation:
The passage contrasts earlier studies that sampled **widely varied alloys and processing conditions** with a later study whose specimens were comparatively homogeneous. Because the later study contained only a narrow range of grain sizes and strengths, the passage suggests that this restricted variation may explain why the previously observed association was not detected. B accurately captures that explanatory purpose.

A is incorrect because the passage does not claim that the earlier relationship is invalid; instead, it offers a reason the later study might not have detected it. C goes beyond the evidence by claiming that annealing temperature is universally more important than grain size. D similarly introduces a specific causal role for nickel that the passage never establishes.

choiceExplanations.B: The passage contrasts earlier studies that sampled **widely varied alloys and processing conditions** with a later study whose specimens were comparatively homogeneous. Because the later study contained only a narrow range of grain sizes and strengths, the passage suggests that this restricted variation may explain why the previously observed association was not detected. B accurately captures that explanatory purpose.

questions.passage: A student is writing an essay about the expansion of rapid-transit systems, arguing that increasing rail capacity may help cities respond to an anticipated widespread change in travel behavior.
questions.question: Which quotation from a publication by a transportation researcher would most effectively support the student’s claim?

choices.A: “Rail passengers consistently rate frequency and reliability among the most important characteristics of a satisfactory transit system.”
choices.B: “As metropolitan populations become denser and private vehicle ownership becomes less practical in many urban cores, the proportion of residents relying on public transportation for routine trips is projected to rise substantially.”
choices.C: “The total amount of energy consumed by an electric train depends partly on the mass of the vehicle, its patterns of acceleration, the number of passengers it carries, and the efficiency of its regenerative braking system.”
choices.D: “Transit agencies frequently redesign station entrances after observing pedestrian congestion during major sporting and cultural events.”

questions.explanation:
The student’s claim concerns a **future widespread change in behavior**—greater use of public transportation—and argues that expanding rail capacity could help cities respond to that change. B directly supports the claim by predicting that a growing share of urban residents will rely on public transit for routine travel.

A concerns qualities riders value but does not establish that transit use will increase. C provides technical information about train energy consumption rather than changes in travel behavior. D describes responses to temporary crowding at particular events, not an expected broad shift in how the public travels.

choiceExplanations.B: The student’s claim concerns a **future widespread change in behavior**—greater use of public transportation—and argues that expanding rail capacity could help cities respond to that change.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from John Dewey’s 1916 nonfiction book *Democracy and Education*.

Education is sometimes treated chiefly as preparation for conditions that lie somewhere in the future, as though the present experience of the learner were valuable only for what it might later produce. <u>Such a view turns the learner’s present life into little more than a means to an end that has not yet arrived.</u> But growth is not merely preparation for some later state; growth itself is a continuing process, and education must therefore find significance in present experience rather than continually postponing it.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It identifies a limitation of an educational approach that Dewey criticizes.
choices.B: It introduces a disagreement among educators that Dewey regards as impossible to resolve.
choices.C: It describes a weakness in learners that Dewey believes formal education must correct.
choices.D: It provides evidence that future-oriented education is more effective than education focused on present experience.

questions.explanation:
The first sentence introduces an approach to education that treats present learning mainly as preparation for the future. The underlined sentence sharpens Dewey’s criticism by explaining a problematic consequence of that approach: it reduces present experience to a mere instrument for some later objective. Thus the sentence **emphasizes a limitation of the educational view Dewey rejects**.

B is incorrect because the passage does not frame the issue as an unresolved controversy among educators. C misidentifies the target of criticism: Dewey is criticizing an educational philosophy, not a defect in learners. D reverses the passage’s position, since Dewey argues against treating present experience merely as preparation for the future.

choiceExplanations.A: The first sentence introduces an approach to education that treats present learning mainly as preparation for the future. The underlined sentence sharpens Dewey’s criticism by explaining a problematic consequence of that approach: it reduces present experience to a mere instrument for some later objective. Thus the sentence **emphasizes a limitation of the educational view Dewey rejects**.

questions.passage: Some archaeological studies reconstruct centuries of regional commerce by mapping the distribution of thousands of ceramic fragments across many settlements. _____ this method with microstratigraphic analysis of residue from a single household hearth may initially seem peculiar, yet both approaches proceed from the assumption that seemingly modest physical traces can reveal much larger patterns of human activity.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: Supplanting
choices.B: Instituting
choices.C: Reconciling
choices.D: Contrasting

questions.explanation:
The sentence places two markedly different archaeological approaches side by side: one examines large-scale ceramic distributions across many sites, whereas the other closely analyzes material from a single hearth. **“Contrasting”** correctly describes the act of comparing those differing approaches before the sentence explains the deeper principle they share.

A, “supplanting,” means replacing one thing with another, which the sentence does not suggest. B, “instituting,” means establishing or introducing a practice. C, “reconciling,” would imply resolving an incompatibility between the two methods, but the sentence simply observes that comparing them may initially seem unusual.

choiceExplanations.D: The sentence places two markedly different archaeological approaches side by side: one examines large-scale ceramic distributions across many sites, whereas the other closely analyzes material from a single hearth. **“Contrasting”** correctly describes the act of comparing those differing approaches before the sentence explains the deeper principle they share.

questions.passage: Newly identified minerals do not automatically receive officially recognized names. Researchers generally submit proposed names and analytical evidence to an international mineralogical committee, which evaluates whether each specimen represents a distinct mineral species. For example, several candidate minerals first described in field reports were not formally approved until much later. _____ years can separate a mineral’s initial collection from the acceptance of its official name.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Conversely,
choices.B: Indeed,
choices.C: Similarly,
choices.D: Therefore,

questions.explanation:
The preceding sentences establish that formal mineral naming involves a review process and note examples in which approval occurred considerably later than initial description. The final sentence **reinforces and emphasizes** that point by stating explicitly that the interval can last years. **“Indeed,”** is therefore the most logical transition.

A introduces opposition, but the final sentence confirms rather than contradicts the preceding information. C normally introduces a comparable case, but the last sentence generalizes and emphasizes the same point rather than presenting a separate parallel example. D indicates a direct causal conclusion; although the review process may contribute to delay, the sentence functions primarily as emphatic confirmation, not as a deductive result of the immediately preceding example.

choiceExplanations.B: The preceding sentences establish that formal mineral naming involves a review process and note examples in which approval occurred considerably later than initial description. The final sentence **reinforces and emphasizes** that point by stating explicitly that the interval can last years. **“Indeed,”** is therefore the most logical transition.

questions.passage: Transportation economists studying travel patterns have examined whether payment structure influences the variety of destinations riders choose. Under a pay-per-ride system, every additional subway trip imposes another fare, so visiting an unfamiliar neighborhood carries an added monetary cost. An unlimited monthly pass, by contrast, requires the same payment whether its owner makes twenty trips or eighty; after the pass has been purchased, taking an additional trip generally costs the rider nothing. This reasoning suggests that _____
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: riders with unlimited passes would likely travel to a wider variety of destinations than otherwise similar riders paying separately for each trip.
choices.B: transit agencies that replace individual fares with unlimited passes would necessarily collect more total revenue.
choices.C: riders who pay for individual trips would be more likely than pass holders to travel over the course of peak commuting hours.
choices.D: unlimited-pass holders would generally take longer individual trips because distance rather than frequency determines the cost of each journey.

questions.explanation:
The passage focuses on the **marginal cost of making an additional trip**. For riders who pay separately, experimenting with another destination requires spending additional money. For unlimited-pass holders, an extra trip usually imposes no additional fare. That difference makes it reasonable to infer that unlimited-pass users would be more willing to make trips to a wider range of destinations.

B is unsupported because nothing in the passage establishes how the fare systems affect total agency revenue. C introduces peak-hour travel, which is never discussed. D is incorrect because the passage says the pass removes the additional cost of another trip; it does not claim that trip distance determines fares or that pass holders take longer trips.

choiceExplanations.A: The passage focuses on the **marginal cost of making an additional trip**. For riders who pay separately, experimenting with another destination requires spending additional money. For unlimited-pass holders, an extra trip usually imposes no additional fare. That difference makes it reasonable to infer that unlimited-pass users would be more willing to make trips to a wider range of destinations.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

- Ganymede is a moon of Jupiter.
- Ganymede has a diameter of approximately 5,268 kilometers.
- Titan is a moon of Saturn.
- Titan has a diameter of approximately 5,150 kilometers.
- Mercury has a diameter of approximately 4,879 kilometers.
- Both Ganymede and Titan are larger in diameter than Mercury.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Ganymede and Titan. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Ganymede, which orbits Jupiter, has a diameter of approximately 5,268 kilometers.
choices.B: Although Ganymede and Titan orbit different planets, each has a diameter greater than that of Mercury.
choices.C: Titan has a diameter of approximately 5,150 kilometers, while Mercury’s diameter is approximately 4,879 kilometers.
choices.D: Ganymede is Jupiter’s moon, whereas Titan orbits Saturn.

questions.explanation:
B directly emphasizes a **shared characteristic**: despite orbiting different planets, both Ganymede and Titan are larger in diameter than Mercury. It therefore accomplishes the student’s stated goal of highlighting a similarity between the two moons.

A discusses only Ganymede and therefore cannot establish a similarity. C compares Titan with Mercury rather than comparing Titan and Ganymede. D emphasizes a difference—the planets the moons orbit—rather than something the two have in common.

choiceExplanations.B:
This choice directly emphasizes a **shared characteristic**: despite orbiting different planets, both Ganymede and Titan are larger in diameter than Mercury. It therefore accomplishes the student’s stated goal of highlighting a similarity between the two moons.

A discusses only Ganymede and therefore cannot establish a similarity. C compares Titan with Mercury rather than comparing Titan and Ganymede.

questions.passage: Many cephalopods alter their appearance using specialized skin structures. Chromatophores contain pigment and can expand or contract rapidly, iridophores reflect particular wavelengths of light, and leucophores scatter ambient light broadly. In a laboratory experiment, marine biologist Lydia Mathger and her team selectively obscured iridophore activity in cuttlefish and found that certain metallic blue-green patterns became markedly less visible.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It distinguishes several mechanisms of cephalopod camouflage and then argues that one of those mechanisms is more important than the others.
choices.B: It describes characteristics of several cephalopod skin structures and then discusses an experiment involving one of those structures.
choices.C: It presents the results of an experiment and then explains the biological structures responsible for those results.
choices.D: It identifies several colors produced by cuttlefish and then compares the wavelengths associated with those colors.

questions.explanation:
The text first provides background information about **three kinds of cephalopod skin structures**, briefly describing what each does. It then shifts to a specific experiment in which researchers manipulated one of those structures, the iridophores, and observed the resulting change in appearance. Choice B accurately captures that two-part organization.

A is incorrect because the text never argues that iridophores are more important than chromatophores or leucophores. C reverses the actual order: the biological structures are described before the experiment. D is too narrow and inaccurate because the passage classifies skin structures, not colors, and does not compare wavelengths.

choiceExplanations.B: The text first provides background information about **three kinds of cephalopod skin structures**, briefly describing what each does. It then shifts to a specific experiment in which researchers manipulated one of those structures, the iridophores, and observed the resulting change in appearance. Choice B accurately captures that two-part organization.

questions.passage: A seventeenth-century astronomical manuscript preserved in Goa spent centuries in a coastal environment where heat and humidity can accelerate the deterioration of paper. _____ most of its pages remain flexible and readily legible. Conservators attribute this unusual survival partly to the manuscript’s paper, which was manufactured from exceptionally durable bast fibers.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Accordingly,
choices.B: Even so,
choices.C: In addition,
choices.D: For example,

questions.explanation:
The first sentence establishes conditions that would ordinarily be expected to damage the manuscript. The next sentence presents a **surprising contrast**: despite those unfavorable conditions, the pages remain in good condition. **“Even so,”** appropriately signals that concession.

A is incorrect because the manuscript’s preservation is not a logical consequence of prolonged heat and humidity. C merely adds information and fails to express the contrast. D would introduce an example of the previous statement, but the preservation of the manuscript contradicts the expected effect of the conditions rather than exemplifying it.

choiceExplanations.B: The first sentence establishes conditions that would ordinarily be expected to damage the manuscript. The next sentence presents a **surprising contrast**: despite those unfavorable conditions, the pages remain in good condition. **“Even so,”** appropriately signals that concession.

questions.passage: Ecologists have sometimes assumed that fruit-eating birds should concentrate on plants whose fruits contain the greatest concentrations of sugars and lipids. Yet when Camila Ortega and colleagues recorded feeding visits by toucans and related birds in a Panamanian forest, nutritional content was a comparatively weak predictor of which plants the birds visited. Instead, the correspondence between a bird’s gape width and a plant’s fruit diameter was substantially more predictive of feeding interactions.
questions.question: Which statement about the birds’ feeding patterns is most strongly supported by the text?

choices.A: A fruit’s physical compatibility with a bird’s feeding anatomy may lead that bird to visit a plant offering less nutritionally rich fruit instead of one offering richer but less manageable fruit.
choices.B: Birds rely on fruit size only when they cannot determine the nutritional content of fruits before attempting to consume them.
choices.C: Fruit-eating birds consistently choose nutritionally poor plants whenever those plants produce fruits that closely match the birds’ gape widths.
choices.D: Anatomical compatibility determines feeding patterns, whereas the nutritional composition of fruit has no relationship whatsoever to which plants birds visit.

questions.explanation:
The study found that **gape-width–fruit-size compatibility predicted feeding interactions more strongly than nutritional content did**. It is therefore reasonable to infer that a bird might select a physically compatible fruit even when another available fruit provides a greater nutritional reward. A expresses that possibility without overstating the evidence.

B is unsupported because the text says nothing about whether birds know the nutritional value of fruits in advance. C is too absolute: the findings indicate a stronger predictive relationship, not that birds *consistently* choose nutritionally poorer fruits. D likewise overstates the result by claiming nutrition has no relationship at all; the passage says nutritional content was a **comparatively weak predictor**, not a nonexistent one.

choiceExplanations.A: The study found that **gape-width–fruit-size compatibility predicted feeding interactions more strongly than nutritional content did**. It is therefore reasonable to infer that a bird might select a physically compatible fruit even when another available fruit provides a greater nutritional reward. A expresses that possibility without overstating the evidence.

questions.passage: “Assisted migration” is a conservation strategy in which organisms are deliberately moved to environments expected to remain suitable as climate conditions change. Ecologist Marissa Chen and colleagues systematically reviewed studies of several assisted-migration approaches, including moving populations toward cooler portions of their existing geographic ranges, establishing populations beyond their historical ranges, and transferring organisms to higher elevations. The reviewers found that **poleward within-range relocation** and **higher-elevation relocation** produced the most consistently favorable results for survival and population establishment.
questions.question: According to the text, which two assisted-migration approaches did Chen and colleagues conclude were most consistently successful?

choices.A: Establishment beyond historical ranges and higher-elevation relocation
choices.B: Poleward within-range relocation and establishment beyond historical ranges
choices.C: Poleward within-range relocation and higher-elevation relocation
choices.D: Higher-elevation relocation and long-distance transcontinental transfer

questions.explanation:
The final sentence explicitly identifies **poleward within-range relocation** and **higher-elevation relocation** as the two approaches associated with the most consistently favorable outcomes. Therefore, C directly matches the information in the text.

A incorrectly substitutes establishment beyond the historical range for poleward relocation. B includes poleward relocation but pairs it with the wrong second method. D includes higher-elevation relocation but introduces “long-distance transcontinental transfer,” which the passage does not identify as one of the reviewed methods.

choiceExplanations.C: The final sentence explicitly identifies **poleward within-range relocation** and **higher-elevation relocation** as the two approaches associated with the most consistently favorable outcomes. Therefore, C directly matches the information in the text.

questions.passage: Although it would be excessive to describe the economic consequences of prolonged port closures as uniformly _____, several analyses suggest that even severe disruptions can produce surprisingly limited effects on national output when freight is rapidly rerouted. During one six-week closure, for example, nearby ports absorbed much of the displaced cargo, and quarterly GDP declined only marginally.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: devastating
choices.B: derivative
choices.C: anomalous
choices.D: negligible

questions.explanation: **“Devastating”** means causing severe damage. The passage says that even severe port closures can sometimes have only limited effects on national output when cargo is rerouted, so describing their consequences as uniformly devastating would overstate the evidence. B, “derivative,” means imitative or originating from something else and does not describe the magnitude of an economic effect. C, “anomalous,” means unusual or inconsistent with a pattern, which is not the issue being discussed. D, “negligible,” means so small as to be unimportant; the passage does not claim that the effects of port closures are always negligible.

choiceExplanations.A: **“Devastating”** means causing severe damage. The passage says that even severe port closures can sometimes have only limited effects on national output when cargo is rerouted, so describing their consequences as uniformly devastating would overstate the evidence.

questions.passage: Foresters often describe a mature tree by its total height. For timber production, however, total height may not accurately indicate how much long, uninterrupted trunk is available: a tree’s **clear bole length**, measured from its base to the first major branch, can be substantially smaller. For example, _____
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?

choices.A: *Eucalyptus regnans* reaches a total height of 76 meters but has a clear bole length of only 28 meters.
choices.B: *Entandrophragma cylindricum* has a 31-meter clear bole and grows primarily in Central Africa.
choices.C: *Cedrela odorata* has a total height of 39 meters, whereas *Agathis australis* reaches 44 meters.
choices.D: *Dipterocarpus grandiflorus* has a clear bole length of 18 meters, considerably less than the 31-meter clear bole of *Entandrophragma cylindricum*.

questions.explanation:
The sentence needs an example showing that **total height and clear bole length can differ substantially for the same tree**. *Eucalyptus regnans* has the greatest total height in the table, 76 meters, but its clear bole extends only 28 meters. That 48-meter difference directly illustrates the distinction the passage describes.

B provides a clear-bole measurement and a geographic fact but does not compare the two relevant measurements. C compares the total heights of two species rather than total height with clear bole length. D compares clear-bole lengths between two species, so it also fails to illustrate how the two measures can differ within one tree species.

table.caption: Dimensions of Selected Commercial Timber Trees

choiceExplanations.A: The sentence needs an example showing that **total height and clear bole length can differ substantially for the same tree**. *Eucalyptus regnans* has the greatest total height in the table, 76 meters, but its clear bole extends only 28 meters. That 48-meter difference directly illustrates the distinction the passage describes.

questions.passage: Although electrospun polymer membranes are prized partly for their microscopic pore structures, the orientation of their fibers can also _____ the material with substantial tensile strength. When fibers are aligned rather than deposited randomly, stresses are distributed more efficiently along the membrane’s principal axis.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: divest
choices.B: endow
choices.C: delimit
choices.D: belie

questions.explanation:
To **endow something with** a quality is to provide or equip it with that quality. The second sentence explains that aligned fibers enable stresses to be distributed more efficiently, thereby giving the membrane substantial tensile strength. “Endow” therefore fits both the meaning and the grammatical construction **“endow the material with.”**

A, “divest,” means deprive and generally takes “of,” not “with”; it would also contradict the strengthening effect. C, “delimit,” means establish a boundary or limit, which does not fit. D, “belie,” means contradict or give a misleading impression of, and the construction “belie the material with strength” is both semantically and grammatically inappropriate.

choiceExplanations.B: To **endow something with** a quality is to provide or equip it with that quality. The second sentence explains that aligned fibers enable stresses to be distributed more efficiently, thereby giving the membrane substantial tensile strength. “Endow” therefore fits both the meaning and the grammatical construction **“endow the material with.”**

questions.passage: Researchers studying digital reading presented participants with two versions of the same dense technical article: one with conventional spacing and one with unusually wide spacing between lines. Participants reading the widely spaced version scrolled more slowly and made fewer rapid cursor movements. Because slower interaction can accompany reduced cognitive load, the researchers concluded that the wider spacing made the article easier to process. A critic noted, however, that slower scrolling can also occur when readers are struggling with difficult material and argued that the wider spacing may instead have increased processing difficulty.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the critic’s claim?

choices.A: Readers in both conditions had encountered articles on similar technical topics before participating in the experiment.
choices.B: Greater processing difficulty is generally associated with increased rereading and backward scrolling, but participants using the widely spaced version exhibited substantially less of both behaviors.
choices.C: Participants reported that they preferred the visual appearance of the conventional version to that of the widely spaced version.
choices.D: Rapid cursor movement has been found to correlate with impatience in some forms of online shopping.

questions.explanation:
The critic argues that **slower scrolling may indicate greater processing difficulty rather than easier processing**. B provides an independent behavioral indicator: if difficulty normally causes more rereading and backward scrolling, but those behaviors actually decreased in the wide-spacing condition, then the difficulty explanation becomes less plausible.

A does not distinguish between the competing explanations because prior familiarity was similar in both groups. C concerns aesthetic preference rather than processing difficulty. D discusses cursor movement in a different context and does not address whether the widely spaced article was cognitively easier or harder to process.

choiceExplanations.B: The critic argues that **slower scrolling may indicate greater processing difficulty rather than easier processing**.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

- “EGOT” refers to winning an Emmy Award, a Grammy Award, an Academy Award (Oscar), and a Tony Award.
- Each award recognizes achievement in a different branch of entertainment.
- A person who wins all four competitive awards is commonly described as an EGOT winner.
- Whoopi Goldberg completed the four-award combination in 2002.
- Goldberg received an Oscar for *Ghost*.
- She received a Tony as a producer of *Thoroughly Modern Millie*.
questions.question: The student wants to explain the EGOT achievement to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Whoopi Goldberg became an EGOT winner in 2002 after earning awards in several areas of entertainment, including an Oscar for *Ghost*.
choices.B: To achieve an EGOT, a person must win all four major entertainment honors represented by the acronym: an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar, and a Tony.
choices.C: Whoopi Goldberg received both an Academy Award for her acting and a Tony Award for her work as a producer before becoming widely known as an EGOT winner.
choices.D: Because the Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony recognize different branches of entertainment, performers such as Whoopi Goldberg can qualify for several of them.

questions.explanation:
The audience is unfamiliar with the achievement, so the most useful response should **define what completing an EGOT requires**. B does exactly that by identifying all four awards and explaining that winning each one constitutes the achievement.

A gives an example but does not fully explain the requirement. C supplies details about only two of the four awards and assumes the audience already understands what “EGOT” means. D explains that the awards cover different areas but does not state that a person must win **all four** to become an EGOT winner.

choiceExplanations.B: The audience is unfamiliar with the achievement, so the most useful response should **define what completing an EGOT requires**.

questions.passage: During a 2021 survey of deep-sea corals near the Azores, marine biologist Sofia Mendes and her colleagues documented twelve *Desmophyllum pertusum* _____ to the family Caryophylliidae, *D. pertusum* can form extensive reef structures in cold, deep water.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: colonies belonging
choices.B: colonies, belonging
choices.C: colonies and belonging
choices.D: colonies. Belonging

questions.explanation:
The first portion forms a complete sentence: “During a 2021 survey ... Mendes and her colleagues documented twelve colonies of *Desmophyllum pertusum*.” The next portion begins with the participial phrase **“Belonging to the family Caryophylliidae,”** which correctly modifies the subject of the new sentence, *D. pertusum*. A period is therefore required between the two sentences.

A would produce a comma splice later in the sentence: “Mendes ... documented twelve colonies belonging to the family Caryophylliidae, *D. pertusum* can form....” B has the same problem and additionally treats “belonging” as supplementary information about the colonies. C creates faulty coordination because “documented” and “belonging” cannot be linked by “and” in that structure.

choiceExplanations.D: The first portion forms a complete sentence: “During a 2021 survey ... Mendes and her colleagues documented twelve colonies of *Desmophyllum pertusum*.” The next portion begins with the participial phrase **“Belonging to the family Caryophylliidae,”** which correctly modifies the subject of the new sentence, *D. pertusum*. A period is therefore required between the two sentences.

questions.passage: Producing extremely compact reference works can require editors to balance legibility against the amount of information placed on each page. The 2012 print edition of the *Handbook of Mediterranean Inscriptions* contains approximately 410,000 words across 820 pages, whereas the 2017 *Encyclopedia of Polar Navigation* contains roughly 525,000 words across 875 pages. These figures suggest that _____
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the original-language sources used in the *Handbook of Mediterranean Inscriptions* contain fewer words than their translated versions.
choices.B: the *Encyclopedia of Polar Navigation* was necessarily more expensive for a publisher to print than the *Handbook of Mediterranean Inscriptions*.
choices.C: the *Encyclopedia of Polar Navigation* contains, on average, more words per page than the *Handbook of Mediterranean Inscriptions*.
choices.D: readers would need approximately the same amount of time to finish both works.

questions.explanation:
The *Handbook of Mediterranean Inscriptions* averages about 500 words per page: 410,000 ÷ 820 = 500. The *Encyclopedia of Polar Navigation* averages about 600 words per page: 525,000 ÷ 875 = 600. Therefore, the latter contains more words per page on average.

A is unsupported because the passage provides no comparison between original-language sources and translations. B cannot be concluded from page and word counts alone because printing cost depends on many other variables. D is likewise unsupported: reading time depends on difficulty, layout, reader speed, and other factors not given.

choiceExplanations.C: The *Handbook of Mediterranean Inscriptions* averages about 500 words per page: 410,000 ÷ 820 = 500. The *Encyclopedia of Polar Navigation* averages about 600 words per page: 525,000 ÷ 875 = 600. Therefore, the latter contains more words per page on average.

questions.passage: Containing an estimated 81 percent iron by mass, _____
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: laboratory researchers classified the Okahandja meteorite, recovered in Namibia, as an iron meteorite.
choices.B: the classification assigned by laboratory researchers places the Okahandja meteorite, recovered in Namibia, among iron meteorites.
choices.C: the Okahandja meteorite, recovered in Namibia, was classified by laboratory researchers as an iron meteorite.
choices.D: among the specimens laboratory researchers classify as iron meteorites is the Okahandja meteorite, recovered in Namibia.

questions.explanation:
The introductory participial phrase **“Containing an estimated 81 percent iron by mass”** must logically modify the noun that immediately follows it. The thing containing that iron is **the Okahandja meteorite**, so C correctly places that noun immediately after the introductory modifier.

A incorrectly suggests that the laboratory researchers contain 81 percent iron. B makes “the classification” the grammatical subject modified by the opening phrase, illogically implying that the classification contains iron. D similarly places “among the specimens” after the modifier rather than directly identifying the meteorite as the thing containing the iron.

choiceExplanations.C: The introductory participial phrase **“Containing an estimated 81 percent iron by mass”** must logically modify the noun that immediately follows it. The thing containing that iron is **the Okahandja meteorite**, so C correctly places that noun immediately after the introductory modifier.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Helena March’s 1908 play *The Orchard Gate*. Clara and Edwin have met on a village road as Edwin prepares to attend an outdoor concert.

**EDWIN:** If the clouds hold, I shall hear the quartet before supper. The organizers have even put chairs beneath the chestnut trees.

**CLARA:** Then take an umbrella. Whenever I go anywhere without one, rain begins before I have gone half a mile.

**EDWIN:** Clara, if the sky stayed blue from April until November, I believe you would carry a cracked parasol merely so that you might complain of the sun coming through it.

Published geochemical work indicates that ²⁰⁶Pb/²⁰⁴Pb ratios above **18.30** in this volcanic province generally indicate incorporation of material from old continental crust, while progressively higher ratios indicate a larger crustal contribution. The crystal core formed first, followed by the rim and then the surrounding matrix.

The student concludes that the rock sample _____
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the student’s conclusion?

choices.A: records a progressively decreasing but persistent contribution from continental crust during its formation.
choices.B: contains isotope ratios too similar across its growth zones to reveal meaningful changes in magma composition.
choices.C: records an increasing contribution from continental crust in each successive stage of mineral growth.
choices.D: began forming without continental-crust influence but acquired such influence during later stages.

questions.explanation:
All three ratios are above the stated **18.30 threshold**, so all three stages indicate some contribution from old continental crust. However, the ratio decreases from **19.42** in the core to **18.96** in the rim and then to **18.61** in the matrix. Because higher values correspond to a larger crustal contribution, the data indicate that this contribution **declined over time but never disappeared**.

B is incorrect because the systematic decline is large enough, under the information supplied, to indicate a changing contribution. C reverses the trend: the ratios decrease rather than increase. D is incorrect because even the earliest zone, the core, has a value well above 18.30 and therefore already indicates crustal influence.

choiceExplanations.A: All three ratios are above the stated **18.30 threshold**, so all three stages indicate some contribution from old continental crust. However, the ratio decreases from **19.42** in the core to **18.96** in the rim and then to **18.61** in the matrix. Because higher values correspond to a larger crustal contribution, the data indicate that this contribution **declined over time but never disappeared**.
choiceExplanations.B: B is incorrect because the systematic decline is large enough, under the information supplied, to indicate a changing contribution.
choiceExplanations.C: C reverses the trend: the ratios decrease rather than increase.
choiceExplanations.D: D is incorrect because even the earliest zone, the core, has a value well above 18.30 and therefore already indicates crustal influence.

questions.passage: In the 1870s, engineer Émile Delacroix replaced the rigid iron vanes on a tidal-current instrument with thin, flexible bronze blades. choices.B: however its
choices.C: however and its

questions.explanation:
The first statement can stand as a complete sentence: “The alteration seemed almost cosmetic, however.” The next statement, beginning with **“Its revised blade geometry,”** is another independent sentence. A period after “however” correctly separates the two.

A creates a comma splice: “The alteration seemed almost cosmetic” and “its revised blade geometry allowed...” are both independent clauses and cannot be joined merely with commas around “however.” B lacks necessary punctuation around “however” and also runs two independent clauses together. C produces illogical coordination because “and” cannot properly connect “however” to the following independent clause.

choices.B: the development by materials chemist Noura El-Sayed involved

D makes “improved charge transport” the apparent recipient, producing the same dangling-modifier problem.

questions.passage: As cultural geographer Amara Velasco explains, several traditional salt varieties from coastal regions are valued for their geographic specificity; _____ consumers prize them because their mineral composition and production methods are closely associated with particular local environments.

A signals a concession, but there is no contradiction. C is generally used to correct or replace a previous formulation, which is not happening here. D signals a result, whereas the second clause explains the meaning of the first rather than presenting a consequence of it.

choiceExplanations.A: A signals a concession, but there is no contradiction.

questions.passage: Modern cybersecurity systems can automatically isolate a compromised server from the rest of a network, preventing suspicious traffic from spreading. There is good reason, however, that administrators configure such systems to act _____: disconnecting a server can interrupt legitimate services and erase access to data needed for ongoing operations, so isolation is most advantageous when there is evidence of an active threat.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: indiscriminately
choices.B: reactively
choices.C: gratuitously
choices.D: unremittingly

questions.explanation:
**“Reactively”** means in response to a particular event or stimulus. The passage explains that isolating a server is costly and therefore most useful **when evidence of an active threat appears**. A reactive system waits for such a threat before taking disruptive action.

A, “indiscriminately,” means without making careful distinctions and would conflict with the passage’s emphasis on acting only when warranted. C, “gratuitously,” means without sufficient reason and likewise contradicts the logic. D, “unremittingly,” means continuously or without stopping, which would make little sense for an action that should occur only when needed.

choiceExplanations.A: A, “indiscriminately,” means without making careful distinctions and would conflict with the passage’s emphasis on acting only when warranted.
choiceExplanations.B: **“Reactively”** means in response to a particular event or stimulus. The passage explains that isolating a server is costly and therefore most useful **when evidence of an active threat appears**. A reactive system waits for such a threat before taking disruptive action.
choiceExplanations.C: C, “gratuitously,” means without sufficient reason and likewise contradicts the logic.
choiceExplanations.D: D, “unremittingly,” means continuously or without stopping, which would make little sense for an action that should occur only when needed.

questions.passage: A large museum once required timed tickets for several of its most popular galleries during peak periods, from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. and from 3:00 to 5:00 p.m. When the requirement was eliminated, administrators expected wait times to increase during those periods in galleries that had previously used timed entry. Surprisingly, wait times also increased substantially outside the former peak periods and in galleries that had never required timed tickets. The data most clearly reflect this unexpected effect during _____

choices.A: 10:00 a.m.–1:00 p.m. for the previously timed galleries.
choices.B: 1:00–3:00 p.m. for the galleries that had never used timed tickets.
choices.C: 3:00–5:00 p.m. for the previously timed galleries.
choices.D: 5:00–6:00 p.m. for both types of galleries.

questions.explanation: The unexpected pattern involves **both conditions** highlighted in the passage: increased waiting outside the former peak periods **and** increased waiting in galleries that had never been subject to timed entry. From 5:00 to 6:00 p.m., which is outside the former peak periods, wait times rise substantially for both previously timed galleries (1.8 minutes) and never-timed galleries (1.3 minutes). This makes B the strongest illustration.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice and C describe increases during the exact peak periods in which administrators already expected previously timed galleries to become more congested.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice shows an increase in never-timed galleries outside the peak period, but the increase is smaller and does not capture the striking simultaneous rise in both gallery types as clearly as B does.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice and C describe increases during the exact peak periods in which administrators already expected previously timed galleries to become more congested.
choiceExplanations.D: The unexpected pattern involves **both conditions** highlighted in the passage: increased waiting outside the former peak periods **and** increased waiting in galleries that had never been subject to timed entry. From 5:00 to 6:00 p.m., which is outside the former peak periods, wait times rise substantially for both previously timed galleries (1.8 minutes) and never-timed galleries (1.3 minutes). This makes B the strongest illustration.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

- In the 1940s, the Colonial Forestry Research Unit in Malaya focused heavily on identifying timber species useful for export.
- Some researchers supported this commercially oriented model.
- Other researchers argued that forestry studies should also incorporate soil science, watershed ecology, and Indigenous land-use practices.
- Malaya became independent in 1957.
- In the early 1960s, botanist Idris Hamzah reorganized the unit as an interdisciplinary Tropical Ecosystems Institute with a stronger emphasis on locally directed research.
- Hamzah’s reforms formed part of a broader post-1945 movement in Asia and Africa to restructure scientific institutions inherited from colonial governments.
questions.question: The student wants to place Hamzah’s reorganization of the institute in historical context. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Researchers at the Colonial Forestry Research Unit disagreed over whether forestry research should remain focused on commercially valuable timber.
choices.B: After Malaya’s 1957 independence, Hamzah reorganized the institute around interdisciplinary, locally directed research, aligning the change with a wider postwar movement to reshape colonial scientific institutions.
choices.C: Hamzah’s early-1960s reforms added soil science and watershed ecology to a research program that had previously emphasized timber species.
choices.D: The Colonial Forestry Research Unit was established before Malaya became independent and included researchers with differing ideas with regard to the proper scope of forestry science.

questions.explanation:
The goal is not simply to describe **what** Hamzah changed but to place the reorganization within a **larger historical setting**. B does this by connecting the early-1960s reform to Malaya’s 1957 independence and to the broader postwar restructuring of colonial scientific institutions.

A explains an internal intellectual disagreement but not the broader historical context. C accurately summarizes part of the reform but omits independence and the wider decolonizing movement. D supplies background chronology but does not connect Hamzah’s reorganization to the broader historical trend.

choiceExplanations.A: A explains an internal intellectual disagreement but not the broader historical context.
choiceExplanations.B: The goal is not simply to describe **what** Hamzah changed but to place the reorganization within a **larger historical setting**.
choiceExplanations.C: C accurately summarizes part of the reform but omits independence and the wider decolonizing movement.
choiceExplanations.D: D supplies background chronology but does not connect Hamzah’s reorganization to the broader historical trend.

choices.A: Orchestra Aurora, which presented more than 80 concerts in both seasons.
choices.B: Orchestra Cadenza, which presented fewer concerts in 2022–23 than in 2012–13.

The administrator claims that **some orchestras increased** their number of subscription concerts. Orchestra Borealis did exactly that, rising from **67** concerts in 2012–13 to **84** in 2022–23.

A does not demonstrate an increase and in fact refers to Orchestra Aurora, whose total declined. B directly contradicts the administrator’s claim because Cadenza decreased. C compares two different orchestras in different seasons rather than showing that a single orchestra increased over time.

choiceExplanations.A: A does not demonstrate an increase and in fact refers to Orchestra Aurora, whose total declined.
choiceExplanations.B: B directly contradicts the administrator’s claim because Cadenza decreased.
choiceExplanations.C: C compares two different orchestras in different seasons rather than showing that a single orchestra increased over time.
choiceExplanations.D: The administrator claims that **some orchestras increased** their number of subscription concerts. Orchestra Borealis did exactly that, rising from **67** concerts in 2012–13 to **84** in 2022–23.

A would introduce a finite verb, “has challenged,” before the sentence’s actual subject and main verb, disrupting the grammatical structure. C creates the same problem in the simple past. D is additionally incorrect in number because the singular panel would require “has,” not “have,” even if a finite verb were appropriate there.

choiceExplanations.C: C creates the same problem in the simple past.
choiceExplanations.D: D is additionally incorrect in number because the singular panel would require “has,” not “have,” even if a finite verb were appropriate there.

questions.passage: Some aviation-safety researchers advocate what is known as a “just culture,” in which pilots, mechanics, and air-traffic personnel can report errors and near misses without automatically being punished for every mistake. Such reporting is important because aviation safety systems improve when investigators can identify recurring weaknesses before those weaknesses contribute to major accidents. If employees fear that acknowledging an error will necessarily damage their careers, they may withhold information that could expose a systemic problem. A strong reporting culture can therefore make accident prevention more efficient.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To identify a specific procedural mistake commonly made by aviation personnel
choices.B: To provide examples of employees who reported errors despite the possibility of punishment
choices.C: To explain the importance of a reporting culture that encourages aviation personnel to acknowledge mistakes and near misses
choices.D: To describe the procedures investigators use to determine responsibility after an aviation accident

questions.explanation:
The passage defines a **just culture** and then explains why it matters: open reporting helps investigators detect recurring systemic problems, whereas fear of punishment can suppress useful information. Its primary purpose is therefore to explain the value of encouraging aviation personnel to report errors and near misses.

A is too narrow because no particular operational mistake is identified. B is incorrect because the passage gives no examples of individual employees. D concerns post-accident investigation procedures, whereas the passage focuses on reporting practices that can help identify risks **before** major accidents occur.

choiceExplanations.A: A is too narrow because no particular operational mistake is identified.
choiceExplanations.B: B is incorrect because the passage gives no examples of individual employees.
choiceExplanations.C: The passage defines a **just culture** and then explains why it matters: open reporting helps investigators detect recurring systemic problems, whereas fear of punishment can suppress useful information. Its primary purpose is therefore to explain the value of encouraging aviation personnel to report errors and near misses.
choiceExplanations.D: D concerns post-accident investigation procedures, whereas the passage focuses on reporting practices that can help identify risks **before** major accidents occur.

questions.passage: Long blamed by municipal officials for accelerating commercial decline, vacant storefronts are often portrayed as causes of neighborhood deterioration. Urban economists Mireille Laurent and Samuel Ortiz, however, argue that such accounts _____ Empty shops frequently appear only after prolonged reductions in pedestrian traffic, credit availability, and local investment; the vacancies may therefore be symptoms of deterioration that was already underway.
questions.question: Which choice best completes the main argument presented in the text?

choices.A: may mistake a consequence for its underlying cause.
choices.B: rely too heavily on unusually prosperous commercial districts.
choices.C: underestimate how rapidly commercial rents can increase.
choices.D: are generally based on evidence collected from too few neighborhoods.

questions.explanation:
The passage explains that vacant storefronts are often blamed for neighborhood decline but may actually **appear after other forces have already caused that decline**. In other words, observers may treat an effect—the vacancies—as though it were the cause. A states that reasoning directly.

B is unsupported because the passage says nothing about unusually prosperous districts. C concerns rents, which are not discussed. D raises a sample-size problem, but the argument is about causal direction, not the amount of evidence collected.

choiceExplanations.A: The passage explains that vacant storefronts are often blamed for neighborhood decline but may actually **appear after other forces have already caused that decline**. In other words, observers may treat an effect—the vacancies—as though it were the cause.
choiceExplanations.B: B is unsupported because the passage says nothing about unusually prosperous districts.
choiceExplanations.C: C concerns rents, which are not discussed.
choiceExplanations.D: D raises a sample-size problem, but the argument is about causal direction, not the amount of evidence collected.

questions.passage: Although handwriting-recognition software often performs well on archival pages written in a consistent script, this pattern might suggest that standardized nineteenth-century shipping ledgers would be especially _____ to automated transcription. Yet archivist Renata Oliveira and colleagues found that abbreviated cargo codes, overwritten figures, and dense marginal calculations generated substantial error rates even in otherwise uniform ledgers.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: refractory
choices.B: ancillary
choices.C: amenable
choices.D: detrimental

questions.explanation:
**“Amenable to”** means suitable for, responsive to, or readily handled by something. If standardized handwriting generally improves recognition accuracy, one might expect standardized ledgers to be especially **amenable to automated transcription**.

A, “refractory,” means resistant or difficult to manage, the opposite of the expectation described. B, “ancillary,” means supplementary or secondary and does not fit the construction. D, “detrimental,” means harmful and would require a different grammatical and logical relationship.

choiceExplanations.A: A, “refractory,” means resistant or difficult to manage, the opposite of the expectation described.
choiceExplanations.B: B, “ancillary,” means supplementary or secondary and does not fit the construction.
choiceExplanations.C: **“Amenable to”** means suitable for, responsive to, or readily handled by something. If standardized handwriting generally improves recognition accuracy, one might expect standardized ledgers to be especially **amenable to automated transcription**.
choiceExplanations.D: D, “detrimental,” means harmful and would require a different grammatical and logical relationship.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**

Catalogers studying marginal annotations in late medieval manuscripts have reported that signed comments by women appear more frequently in manuscripts produced in northern Italy than in those copied in England. Based on surveys of several monastic and household collections, historians Eliana Moretti and Peter Graves have suggested that women may have participated more visibly in manuscript reading communities in northern Italy.

**Text 2**

Book historian Amina Qureshi cautions that the apparent regional difference may partly reflect preservation and detection. English readers often added notes in iron-gall ink near page edges, where trimming and fading disproportionately erased them; some Italian collections, by contrast, preserve darker annotations placed farther from the margins. Qureshi argues that surviving counts may therefore underrepresent annotations in the English manuscripts.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 about the different prevalence of women’s annotations?

choices.A: By arguing that the regional difference may partly result from differences in how easily the annotations survive and can be detected.
choices.B: By agreeing that the regional difference is genuine but arguing that women in England generally read different genres of manuscripts.
choices.C: By suggesting that Italian manuscript collections have been studied less extensively than English ones.
choices.D: By claiming that signed annotations are unreliable evidence of whether women participated in manuscript culture at all.

questions.explanation:
Text 2 does not necessarily deny that a regional difference exists. Instead, it proposes a **detection and preservation bias**: English annotations may have disappeared more often because of fading and trimming. Thus the apparent difference in prevalence could partly reflect how readily evidence survives and is observed.

B introduces differences in reading genres that Text 2 never mentions. C reverses the concern; Text 2 focuses on preservation, not uneven scholarly attention. D is too sweeping because Text 2 questions the completeness of surviving counts, not the usefulness of signed annotations altogether.

choiceExplanations.A: Text 2 does not necessarily deny that a regional difference exists. Instead, it proposes a **detection and preservation bias**: English annotations may have disappeared more often because of fading and trimming. Thus the apparent difference in prevalence could partly reflect how readily evidence survives and is observed.
choiceExplanations.B: B introduces differences in reading genres that Text 2 never mentions.
choiceExplanations.C: C reverses the concern; Text 2 focuses on preservation, not uneven scholarly attention.
choiceExplanations.D: D is too sweeping because Text 2 questions the completeness of surviving counts, not the usefulness of signed annotations altogether.

questions.passage: Many wind-dispersed tree seeds weigh only a few milligrams or less, which is unsurprising given that low mass can facilitate transport by moving air. But not all wind-dispersed seeds are extremely light, as can be seen most clearly in the example of the _____

A and D identify comparatively heavy seeds, but neither species is primarily wind dispersed. C identifies a wind-dispersed species, but its extremely low seed mass reinforces the usual pattern rather than providing the requested exception.

choiceExplanations.B: The passage needs an example of a seed that is **wind dispersed but relatively heavy**. Silver maple satisfies both conditions: its seeds are primarily wind dispersed and have an average mass of 38.6 mg, far greater than the tiny paper birch seeds.

questions.passage: Oceanographers mapping a hydrothermal field in the western Pacific recorded a narrow patch of unusually warm water several hundred meters downslope from an active vent. No nearby geological feature could readily account for the anomaly, so the researchers hypothesized that the warm patch had originated at the vent and had then been carried away by a localized bottom current.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the researchers’ hypothesis?

choices.A: Samples collected inside the warm patch contained fewer suspended mineral particles than samples taken directly above the vent.
choices.B: A time-lapse sequence showed the warm patch gradually shifting farther downslope from the active vent over several hours.
choices.C: The active vent was hotter during the second survey day than it had been during the first.
choices.D: Water temperatures upslope from the vent remained stable throughout the observation period.

questions.explanation:
The hypothesis specifically proposes **movement away from the vent**: the anomalously warm water originated there and was transported downslope. A time-lapse showing the warm patch progressively drifting farther from the vent directly supports that predicted movement.

A provides compositional information but does not show where the patch came from or how it moved. C concerns changes in the vent’s temperature rather than transport of the existing warm patch. D gives information about water in another location and does not establish the patch’s origin or trajectory.

choiceExplanations.A: A provides compositional information but does not show where the patch came from or how it moved.
choiceExplanations.B: The hypothesis specifically proposes **movement away from the vent**: the anomalously warm water originated there and was transported downslope. A time-lapse showing the warm patch progressively drifting farther from the vent directly supports that predicted movement.
choiceExplanations.C: C concerns changes in the vent’s temperature rather than transport of the existing warm patch.
choiceExplanations.D: D gives information about water in another location and does not establish the patch’s origin or trajectory.

questions.passage: A media-studies student is researching a ten-part livestream series that followed the restoration of a badly damaged seventeenth-century astronomical clock. The first nine installments emphasized uncertainty: conservators repeatedly uncovered hidden damage, revised their estimates, and debated whether the original mechanism could ever function again. The student claims that viewers ultimately preferred resolution and closure to prolonged uncertainty.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student’s claim?

choices.A: The restoration team used a substantially larger assortment of specialized imaging equipment during episode 6 than it had used in any of the earlier installments.
choices.B: The final episode, in which the restored clock was successfully restarted and its mechanism explained, attracted more viewers than any previous installment.
choices.C: Professional horologists rated episode 3 as the most technically informative part of the series.
choices.D: Several viewers reported that they began watching the series because they were interested in seventeenth-century astronomy.

questions.explanation:

choices.B: declined gradually because minor defects eventually made most satellites unusable.
choices.C: reached approximately the same overall size as satellite networks that were maintained through entirely different systems of operation.
choices.D: did not fail because catastrophic hardware faults became too prevalent for the network to remain operational.

questions.explanation:
The earlier theory predicted that accumulated serious faults would eventually make the isolated network unsustainable. The simulations instead show that the **most damaging faults became less frequent**, while the network expanded and remained stable until deliberate retirement. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that catastrophic faults did **not** become prevalent enough to cause the network’s failure.

A goes beyond the evidence: fewer catastrophic faults resulted from maintenance, not necessarily from increasing physical resistance. B contradicts the fact that the network maintained roughly seventy active satellites until retirement. C introduces a comparison with other networks that the passage does not provide.

choiceExplanations.A: A goes beyond the evidence: fewer catastrophic faults resulted from maintenance, not necessarily from increasing physical resistance.
choiceExplanations.B: B contradicts the fact that the network maintained roughly seventy active satellites until retirement.
choiceExplanations.C: C introduces a comparison with other networks that the passage does not provide.
choiceExplanations.D: The earlier theory predicted that accumulated serious faults would eventually make the isolated network unsustainable. The simulations instead show that the **most damaging faults became less frequent**, while the network expanded and remained stable until deliberate retirement. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that catastrophic faults did **not** become prevalent enough to cause the network’s failure.

The following text is adapted from Jack London’s 1904 novel *The Sea-Wolf*.

The schooner lay a **good** mile from the gray line of shore, and between us and it the wind had roughened the water into short, steep ridges. Even from the deck, the figures moving beside the distant huts seemed scarcely larger than marks of charcoal.

choices.C: considerable
choices.D: skillful

questions.explanation:
In the phrase **“a good mile,”** “good” indicates that the distance is substantial or fully a mile, perhaps even slightly more. **“Considerable”** therefore most nearly matches its meaning in context.

A refers to moral virtue, which is irrelevant to distance. B describes reliability. D refers to ability or competence. None of those meanings fits a phrase estimating how far offshore the schooner lies.

choiceExplanations.A: A refers to moral virtue, which is irrelevant to distance.
choiceExplanations.B: B describes reliability.
choiceExplanations.C: In the phrase **“a good mile,”** “good” indicates that the distance is substantial or fully a mile, perhaps even slightly more. **“Considerable”** therefore most nearly matches its meaning in context.
choiceExplanations.D: D refers to ability or competence.

choiceExplanations.A: A would tend to make diesel less attractive and thus strengthen the case for battery-electric vans.
choiceExplanations.B: The table identifies **battery-electric vans** as the most profitable option, with an operating margin of €78,000.

questions.passage: Brown dwarfs are sometimes classified according to atmospheric temperature and spectral features. **“Incongruous with”** means inconsistent with or not in harmony with something. The unexpectedly low temperature and methane absorption do not fit the characteristics expected of the original warm L-type classification, so the observations are incongruous with that classification.

A means favorable to or helping produce something, which does not fit. B means representative of, but the observations undermine rather than exemplify the original classification. C means lower in rank or importance than something and does not describe the relationship between evidence and a scientific classification.

choiceExplanations.A: A means favorable to or helping produce something, which does not fit.
choiceExplanations.B: B means representative of, but the observations undermine rather than exemplify the original classification.
choiceExplanations.C: C means lower in rank or importance than something and does not describe the relationship between evidence and a scientific classification.
choiceExplanations.D: **“Incongruous with”** means inconsistent with or not in harmony with something. The unexpectedly low temperature and methane absorption do not fit the characteristics expected of the original warm L-type classification, so the observations are incongruous with that classification.

questions.passage: In the exhibition *Fired Futures*, contemporary ceramicists combine hand-thrown vessels with computer-generated molds, robotic carving, and glazes derived from historical kiln recipes. choiceExplanations.C: The preceding sentence describes the exhibition’s unusual arrangement: historical and digitally fabricated ceramics are placed together rather than separated chronologically. questions.passage: Sylvia Plath’s 1963 novel *The Bell Jar* is often read through an autobiographical lens. The resemblance is understandable: several of Esther Greenwood’s experiences parallel events in Plath’s life. Yet the novel also compresses chronology, invents episodes, and reshapes people and events for artistic purposes. Readers who treat every narrative detail chiefly as evidence about Plath’s biography may therefore _____
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: underestimate how extensively Plath transformed lived experience through imaginative construction.
choices.B: exaggerate the extent to which *The Bell Jar* influenced novels published before 1963.
choices.C: overlook evidence that Plath drew on events from her own life when composing the novel.
choices.D: misjudge how widely *The Bell Jar* was read immediately after publication.

questions.explanation:
The passage acknowledges that the novel contains genuine autobiographical parallels but emphasizes that Plath also **invented, compressed, and reshaped** material. A reader who focuses only on one-to-one correspondences with Plath’s life could therefore fail to appreciate the creative transformation involved in constructing the novel.

B concerns the novel’s influence on earlier works, which is chronologically impossible and unrelated to the passage. C reverses the problem: the passage says such readers focus **too heavily** on autobiographical correspondences, not that they overlook them. D concerns readership and publication history, neither of which is discussed.

choiceExplanations.A: The passage acknowledges that the novel contains genuine autobiographical parallels but emphasizes that Plath also **invented, compressed, and reshaped** material. A reader who focuses only on one-to-one correspondences with Plath’s life could therefore fail to appreciate the creative transformation involved in constructing the novel.
choiceExplanations.B: B concerns the novel’s influence on earlier works, which is chronologically impossible and unrelated to the passage.
choiceExplanations.C: C reverses the problem: the passage says such readers focus **too heavily** on autobiographical correspondences, not that they overlook them.
choiceExplanations.D: D concerns readership and publication history, neither of which is discussed.

questions.passage: Oscar Wilde’s 1895 play *The Importance of Being Earnest* satirizes the self-importance of Britain’s upper classes, sometimes by having wealthy characters casually express expectations that expose the absurdity of the social hierarchy they take for granted.
questions.question: Which quotation from the play most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.B: Lady Bracknell declares, “Really, if the lower orders don’t set us a good example, what on earth is the use of them?”

choices.D: Gwendolen observes, “In matters of grave importance, style, not sincerity, is the vital thing.”

A is paradoxical but concerns truth rather than social rank. C humorously values expression over accuracy but does not expose class assumptions. D satirizes superficiality, yet it does not specifically illustrate the upper-class expectation described in the claim.

choiceExplanations.A: A is paradoxical but concerns truth rather than social rank.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice most directly illustrates aristocratic self-importance. Lady Bracknell absurdly suggests that the purpose of the “lower orders” is to provide a moral example for their social superiors, revealing both her entitlement and the play’s satire of class hierarchy.

questions.passage: Steelhead trout living above and below Washington’s Harlow Falls Dam are now genetically distinct. Because the dam, completed in 1956, prevents most adult fish from moving between the two stretches of river, biologists long attributed the genetic division to the barrier. After analyzing preserved scales collected from the river between 1908 and 1932, however, population geneticist Maren Ishikawa and her colleagues rejected that explanation.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain why Ishikawa and her colleagues rejected the common explanation?

choices.A: During years with unusually heavy rainfall, trout originating in a neighboring river occasionally entered both stretches of the Harlow River at different times.
choices.B: Preserved scales were available from both the upstream and downstream portions of the river beginning in 1908.
choices.C: Two genetically distinct trout lineages entered the Harlow River from different tributaries after the dam was completed.
choices.D: The genetic division found in modern trout closely matched the division already present in specimens collected several decades before the dam was built.

questions.explanation: If the same genetic division existed **before 1956**, the dam cannot have created that division. B therefore directly undermines the idea that the modern population structure arose because the dam blocked movement.

choiceExplanations.A: This choice could complicate current gene flow but does not show that the division predates the dam.
choiceExplanations.B: This choice merely establishes that researchers possessed older samples; it does not state what those samples revealed.
choiceExplanations.C: This choice actually places the origin of the split after dam construction and therefore could support rather than weaken the common explanation.
choiceExplanations.D: If the same genetic division existed **before 1956**, the dam cannot have created that division. B therefore directly undermines the idea that the modern population structure arose because the dam blocked movement.
