Historian Ada Rell later examined twelve libraries that adopted such policies and found substantial increases in borrowing during the two years after each change, suggesting that _____
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: libraries did not experience increased borrowing until at least two years after eligibility expanded.
choices.B: the observed results were consistent with the prevailing expectation about broader eligibility.
choices.C: researchers had failed to anticipate substantial negative effects on collection use.
choices.D: libraries in Lera experienced larger increases than libraries in Norra did.

questions.explanation: B aligns the measured increases with the earlier prediction of greater use. D makes a location-specific comparison unsupported by the aggregate result. A mistakes increases observed during the two-year period for increases that began only after that period. C introduces negative effects absent from the findings and reverses their relationship to the prediction.

questions.passage: “Portraiture” is a 1921 poem by Nessa Rell. The speaker expresses ambivalence about portraits, acknowledging their value while also conveying displeasure with them, writing,
questions.question: Which quotation from “Portraiture” most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: “No ledger of faces / should omit the laborer’s hands; / these too belong within the frame.”
choices.B: “When the borrowed gestures multiply / until no face is legible, / we do not cherish / what we cannot read.”
choices.C: “I turn from portraits with impatience, / yet under the stubborn paint I find / a living truth I cannot wholly scorn.”
choices.D: “A likeness must be distinguished / from a mask: the hurried painter / may mistake the second for the first.”

questions.explanation: C combines impatience with acknowledgment of a valuable “living truth,” directly demonstrating mixed judgment. A argues for inclusion without expressing displeasure. D distinguishes successful and unsuccessful representation without showing the speaker’s opposing feelings. B conveys criticism of an unclear kind of portrait but does not acknowledge its merits.

questions.passage: Associated with a group of early twentieth-century designers known as the Lera Workshop, regional _____ became known for repeated geometric motifs and broad areas of unadorned wood in large storage chests.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: furniture maker Tessa Venn,
choices.B: furniture maker Tessa Venn
choices.C: furniture maker, Tessa Venn,
choices.D: furniture maker, Tessa Venn

questions.explanation: B forms the integrated subject “regional furniture maker Tessa Venn” and connects it directly to “became known.” C incorrectly makes the identifying name parenthetical. A wrongly separates the completed subject from its verb. D inserts an unnecessary comma between the occupational description and its identifying name.

questions.passage: Materials researcher Oren Dall believes that studying how loose pigment grains sometimes form durable pellets may clarify the first stage of a traditional finishing process. Dall’s team reviewed experiments in which the grains were exposed to the additives laren and veska. The team concluded that neither additive was likely to have played a significant role in initiating pellet formation.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team’s conclusion?

choices.A: The grains generally formed pellets after exposure to veska but not after exposure to laren.
choices.B: The grains generally formed pellets after exposure to laren but not after exposure to veska.
choices.C: The grains generally failed to form pellets after exposure to either laren or veska.
choices.D: The grains generally formed pellets after exposure to either laren or veska.

questions.explanation: C shows an absence of the relevant response for both additives, supporting the conclusion that neither initiates pellet formation. D supports a role for both and contradicts the conclusion. B supports a role for laren, while A supports a role for veska; each therefore conflicts with the conclusion that neither has a significant initiating role.

questions.passage: Archaeologist Leona Vardis divided clay tokens from the Merjan warehouses into three groups based on the depth of their incised marks. Her categories were provisional: rather than treating the divisions as established facts, she used them to predict which tokens would occur together in deposits that had not yet been excavated. Discoveries that contradicted those predictions would require her to redraw the categories.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does “provisional” most nearly mean?

choices.A: Definitive
choices.B: Incidental
choices.C: Prescriptive
choices.D: Tentative

questions.explanation: D is correct because Vardis treats the categories as a working arrangement that remains open to revision. Their usefulness lies in producing predictions, not in already being proven. C means intended to prescribe how something should be done; Vardis is classifying existing objects, not issuing rules for making them. B means occurring as a minor or accidental accompaniment, whereas the categories organize the investigation. A means conclusively settled, directly contradicting the statement that contrary discoveries would require revision.

questions.passage: Architectural historian Rafael Solís admired the economy of the roof system in the surviving drawings for the Aster Pavilion. Yet the drawings showed neither the connections between the roof and its supports nor the alterations made during construction. Solís therefore qualified his praise: the design was an elegant solution on paper, he wrote, but its practical success could not be established from the drawings alone.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does “qualified” most nearly mean?

choices.A: Clarified
choices.B: Limited
choices.C: Substantiated
choices.D: Endorsed

questions.explanation: B is correct because Solís attaches a restriction to his favorable judgment: he praises the drawn design while withholding a judgment about its performance as a built structure. D would indicate approval, but the verb describes what he does to that approval after identifying missing evidence. A would mean making the praise easier to understand; the passage instead emphasizes narrowing its scope. C would mean supporting the praise with evidence, whereas the missing construction details prevent him from substantiating practical success.

questions.passage: In photographs of polished stone panels, conservator Mirela Dobre noticed dark bands that seemed to follow the direction of the finishing strokes. One possibility was that the bands were shadows cast by shallow grooves. However, the bands remained in the same locations when the panels were photographed under light arriving from the opposite direction. Dobre next examined whether particles trapped beneath the surface, rather than the surface contours themselves, accounted for the pattern.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence beginning “However, the bands remained” in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It reports an observation that weakens an initial explanation and motivates consideration of another.
choices.B: It identifies a limitation of photography that makes both proposed explanations impossible to evaluate.
choices.C: It establishes that the panels were finished with a technique different from the one Dobre initially suspected.
choices.D: It supplies direct evidence that trapped particles are the sole cause of the bands.

questions.explanation: A is correct because reversing the light direction would be expected to change shadows produced by grooves. The unchanged bands therefore count against the shadow explanation and lead Dobre to investigate subsurface particles. C introduces a conclusion about the finishing technique that the observation does not establish. B incorrectly treats the observation as a methodological failure; it helps distinguish explanations. D overstates the evidence: weakening one explanation does not demonstrate that the alternative is the only possible cause.

questions.passage: Historical nursery catalogs seem to document an extraordinary proliferation of pear varieties in nineteenth-century Bellacosta. Botanist Serena Ocampo found, however, that catalogs sometimes assigned different names to trees with the same fruit characteristics and propagation history. By comparing descriptions with orchard notebooks, she reduced the apparent number of varieties substantially. Ocampo cautions that her revised inventory says little about whether biological diversity increased or decreased during the period; it mainly shows how inconsistently the catalogs recorded that diversity.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Nursery owners deliberately exaggerated the number of pear varieties to conceal the disappearance of older trees.
choices.B: Orchard notebooks demonstrate that pear diversity declined as nursery catalogs became more widely circulated.
choices.C: Reconciling inconsistent historical names can improve an inventory of pear varieties without establishing a historical trend in their diversity.
choices.D: The diversity of nineteenth-century pears cannot be investigated unless researchers locate every surviving nursery catalog.

questions.explanation: C is correct because it combines Ocampo’s main finding—different names inflated the apparent inventory—with her explicit limit on what the revised count can establish. B turns a correction to the recorded count into evidence of an actual biological decline, which Ocampo cautions against. D imposes a requirement to locate every catalog that the text never states. A invents a motive for the inconsistent naming; the passage reports the inconsistency without claiming that nursery owners intended to mislead anyone.

questions.passage: Technician Amara Kibet asked experienced watchmakers and untrained volunteers to identify faults in drawings of clock mechanisms. The watchmakers were much more accurate when the components appeared in their customary positions. When the same components were rearranged into mechanically implausible configurations, however, the watchmakers’ advantage nearly disappeared, although the number and appearance of the components were unchanged. The volunteers performed similarly in both conditions.
questions.question: Which inference is most strongly supported by the text?

choices.A: Training watchmakers to memorize more component names would necessarily restore their advantage with implausible configurations.
choices.B: The volunteers possessed a greater understanding of the mechanisms than the watchmakers did but could demonstrate it only with rearranged components.
choices.C: Rearranging the components eliminated all recognizable visual differences between functioning and faulty mechanisms.
choices.D: The watchmakers’ expertise may depend partly on familiar relationships among components, rather than only on recognizing individual components.

questions.explanation: D is correct because the experts lose much of their advantage when spatial relationships change even though the individual components remain visually the same. That pattern supports a role for familiarity with the overall arrangement. B attributes hidden mechanical expertise to the volunteers without evidence. C overstates the manipulation: faults can still be identified, and the passage does not say all visual differences disappear. A predicts the guaranteed effect of a training intervention that was not tested.

questions.passage: Art historian Inez Carvajal argues that the recurring maritime symbols in the municipal murals of Puerto Neral during the 1940s primarily reflect the preferences of the commercial guilds that financed the projects, rather than the subjects residents most wanted represented. Because residents and guild members sometimes expressed similar preferences, the mere presence of maritime imagery would not, by itself, distinguish the two explanations.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Carvajal’s argument?

choices.A: The murals that contained the most maritime imagery attracted the largest crowds at their unveiling ceremonies.
choices.B: Several residents who praised the murals also worked for companies that belonged to the guilds.
choices.C: Artists whose earlier work featured harbor imagery were more likely than other artists to apply for municipal mural commissions.
choices.D: An artist replaced a proposed market scene with harbor imagery after a financing guild requested the change, although resident surveys continued to favor the market scene.

questions.explanation: D is correct because it isolates a case in which guild preferences and resident preferences diverged, and the final subject followed the funder’s request. That directly supports the claim that financing guilds drove the imagery. B shows overlap between the groups, which makes their influence harder to distinguish. A concerns responses after completion, not whose preferences determined the subject. C concerns who applied for commissions, not whether guild requests or residents’ wishes shaped the commissioned murals.

questions.passage: The Senara Archive’s digital interface allows scholars to compare revisions that are difficult to examine together in its reading room, where fragile manuscripts must be consulted individually. _____ a researcher can display successive drafts of a single treaty on one screen and track a clause as it moves from the opening section to a later appendix.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: In short,
choices.B: For instance,
choices.C: Meanwhile,
choices.D: Conversely,

questions.explanation: B is correct because the second sentence gives a specific example of the comparisons enabled by the interface. D would signal a reversal, but the example supports the preceding claim. A would introduce a summary or restatement; the second sentence instead adds concrete details about one use of the interface. C would establish simultaneity between separate events, whereas the relationship is between a general capability and an illustration of that capability.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
Acoustician Pavel Rudenko compares two methods for measuring a room’s response to sound.
The impulse method uses a brief burst containing many frequencies at once.
The swept-tone method uses a sustained signal whose frequency changes gradually.
Both methods can estimate how strongly a room amplifies different frequencies.
Rudenko used both methods in the same empty concert hall.
questions.question: The student wants to distinguish how the two methods supply sound to the room while acknowledging their shared purpose. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: A brief burst containing many frequencies allows the impulse method to estimate a room’s response to sound.
choices.B: The swept-tone method is more convenient than the impulse method because it uses a sustained signal rather than a brief burst.
choices.C: Rudenko used two methods in an empty concert hall to estimate how strongly the room amplified different frequencies.
choices.D: Although both methods estimate a room’s response across frequencies, the impulse method supplies many frequencies together, whereas the swept-tone method supplies them through a gradually changing signal.

questions.explanation: D is correct because it identifies the shared aim and then directly contrasts the way each method introduces frequencies. C states the common purpose and setting but omits the requested difference. B makes an unsupported claim about convenience and does not acknowledge the shared purpose. A accurately describes one method but does not compare it with the other or explicitly establish their common aim.

questions.passage: The inscriptions on three silver amulets use different abbreviations for the same ceremonial titles. Even after paleographer Yasmin Haddad compared the abbreviations with those in dated manuscripts, the extent to which the variations indicate different places of manufacture, rather than the preferences of individual engravers, _____ uncertain.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have remained
choices.B: remains
choices.C: remain
choices.D: are remaining

questions.explanation: B is correct because the singular head of the subject is “extent,” so the verb must be singular: “the extent ... remains uncertain.” The plural nouns “variations,” “places,” “preferences,” and “engravers” occur within phrases that modify or complete that subject; none controls the main verb’s number. C and A are plural verb forms, and D also requires a plural subject. The intervening description does not change the singular grammatical relationship between “extent” and “remains.”

questions.passage: The acoustic properties of architect Celina Moravec’s unbuilt recital hall are difficult to reconstruct from its surviving plans. The plans specify the dimensions of the main room but omit the materials intended for its curved rear wall_____ several researchers have used them to estimate how sound would have traveled through the hall.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ; nevertheless,
choices.B: , nevertheless,
choices.C: , nevertheless;
choices.D: nevertheless,

questions.explanation: A is correct because a semicolon separates two independent clauses: “The plans specify ... but omit ...” and “several researchers have used them ... .” The conjunctive adverb “nevertheless” introduces the second clause and is followed by a comma. B creates a comma splice; “nevertheless” is not a coordinating conjunction that can join the clauses with a comma alone. D fails to supply a boundary between the independent clauses. C puts the semicolon after the transition while leaving the first clause improperly joined to that transition.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Only a few letters in the surviving correspondence of the Valnera Engineering School describe women attending its public lectures between 1912 and 1920. Most letters mentioning lecture attendance were written by men. This imbalance suggests that women rarely participated in the school’s public scientific culture during that period.
**Text 2**
Correspondence at Valnera was preserved unevenly. A later archive policy retained almost all letters from professional engineers, who were predominantly men, but discarded many letters from other attendees. Attendance lists recovered from a separate municipal collection identify women at numerous public lectures. Counts drawn solely from the school’s surviving letters therefore require caution.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the inference in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the surviving correspondence may reflect selective preservation more strongly than the original pattern of participation
choices.B: By claiming that the municipal attendance lists establish that women outnumbered men at every lecture
choices.C: By suggesting that public lectures had little effect on the school’s scientific culture, regardless of who attended
choices.D: By accepting that women rarely attended while maintaining that their contributions were more scientifically important than men’s

questions.explanation: A is correct because Text 2 identifies a preservation policy that favored letters from a predominantly male professional group and cites independent evidence of women’s attendance. Those points challenge treating the correspondence count as a representative attendance count. D accepts the inference that Text 2 calls into question and adds an unsupported comparison of scientific importance. B exaggerates what the lists establish: they show participation at numerous lectures, not a female majority at every lecture. C changes the issue to the lectures’ influence, which neither text evaluates.

questions.passage: Listeners in a study by cognitive scientist Tobias Mensah heard an unfamiliar melody twice. Between the hearings, one group encountered a slightly altered ending presented as a separate tune. When asked later to reproduce the original melody, many members of that group supplied the altered ending instead. Mensah describes the participants’ auditory memories as plastic: the memories did not simply weaken with time but were reshaped by a subsequent, related experience.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does “plastic” most nearly mean?

choices.A: Precise
choices.B: Persistent
choices.C: Malleable
choices.D: Artificial

questions.explanation: C is correct because the memories change their form in response to later experience: participants incorporate the new ending into their recollection of the earlier melody. “Malleable” captures that capacity to be reshaped. D would mean manufactured or inauthentic, but the participants genuinely heard and remembered a melody. A would mean exact, which conflicts with the substitution of the altered ending. B would emphasize lasting unchanged over time; the passage explicitly distinguishes modification from simple persistence or fading.

questions.passage: Port officials in Darzun revised their cargo forms so that shipments were classified by the residence of the warehouse owner rather than by the location where the goods had been produced. The following year, the forms recorded a sharp decline in foreign cargo. Historian Hana Petrov found that many locally owned warehouses still contained the same kinds and quantities of imported goods as before the revision. Taken together, these findings suggest that _____
questions.question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the recorded decline may have resulted partly from reclassification rather than from a comparable decrease in imports.
choices.B: warehouse owners increasingly preferred imported goods once those goods were classified as local cargo.
choices.C: the form revision caused foreign producers to reduce the quantity of goods they sent to Darzun.
choices.D: locally owned warehouses had begun producing goods that were indistinguishable from imported goods.

questions.explanation: A is correct because goods produced abroad could be counted as local under the new owner-based system. The stable imported inventories support caution about interpreting the lower recorded count as a genuine trade decline. D introduces local manufacture, for which there is no evidence. C predicts an actual decrease in shipments, whereas Petrov’s finding suggests continuity in imported inventories. B infers a change in owners’ preferences even though the reported quantities and kinds remained similar.

questions.passage: Literary psychologist Esra Kalkan found that participants recalled more lines from poems with recurring images than from poems without recurring images. The poems were matched for length and grammatical complexity. Kalkan concluded that recurring imagery independently improves recall, rather than merely accompanying some other feature that makes a poem easier to remember.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Kalkan’s conclusion?

choices.A: Several poems without recurring images were recalled less accurately than poems with recurring images of comparable length.
choices.B: Participants who reported enjoying poetry recalled more lines overall than participants who reported little interest in poetry.
choices.C: Some participants could describe the recurring images in a poem without remembering the order in which those images appeared.
choices.D: When the two sets of poems were also matched for word familiarity, the recall advantage disappeared even though their difference in recurring imagery remained.

questions.explanation: D is correct because controlling another feature—word familiarity—eliminates the effect attributed independently to recurring imagery. That indicates the original advantage may have reflected vocabulary familiarity rather than recurrence itself. B identifies a general difference among readers without explaining the difference between the two sets of poems. A reproduces the original pattern and therefore supports rather than weakens it. C distinguishes remembering images from remembering their sequence, but it does not show that recurring imagery fails to improve line recall.

questions.passage:
**Seed Germination After Seven Days**
Ecologist Noura Bensalem compared untreated seeds with briefly heat-treated seeds from three populations of the same shrub. All seeds were then kept under identical light and water conditions. Bensalem claims that the heat treatment produced the greatest proportional increase in germination for the Tavira Dunes population.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Bensalem’s claim?

choices.A: Germination increased by 20 percentage points in both the Orell Ridge and Sefra Basin samples.
choices.B: The heat-treated seeds from Orell Ridge had a germination rate of 70%, higher than that of either other population.
choices.C: Germination in the Tavira Dunes samples rose from 20% to 60%, tripling, whereas germination in each other population increased by less than double.
choices.D: The heat-treated seeds from Tavira Dunes and Sefra Basin both had germination rates of 60%.

questions.explanation: C is correct because proportional increase depends on the initial rate. Tavira Dunes rises to three times its untreated rate, whereas Orell Ridge rises to 1.4 times its initial rate and Sefra Basin to 1.5 times its initial rate. B identifies the highest final rate, which is different from the greatest proportional improvement. D compares final rates while ignoring different starting rates. A reports the same absolute increase for the two other populations but does not establish which population has the greatest increase relative to its baseline.

questions.passage: The earliest printed edition of Lidia Ferran’s choral work groups its lines into regular stanzas, a feature that later critics treated as evidence of the composer’s preference for symmetrical phrasing. _____ a manuscript prepared by Ferran’s copyist places several of those same lines within uninterrupted musical phrases, suggesting that the printed divisions may reflect an editor’s layout decisions rather than the composer’s intended structure.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: In other words,
choices.B: Furthermore,
choices.C: However,
choices.D: As a result,

questions.explanation: C is correct because the manuscript evidence challenges the interpretation based on the printed edition. The two sources do not simply provide additional support for the same conclusion. D would imply that the manuscript’s phrasing resulted from the critics’ interpretation, a causal relationship the passage does not suggest. A would introduce a restatement, but the second sentence revises the explanation of the divisions. B would signal an additional supporting point rather than evidence that calls the earlier interpretation into question.

questions.passage: Comparing recordings made thirty years apart and excluding changes attributable to the recording equipment, _____
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: linguist Anika Vermeer identified several shifts in the pronunciation of unstressed vowels in the speech of the island’s residents.
choices.B: the pronunciation of unstressed vowels had undergone several shifts, according to linguist Anika Vermeer’s analysis of the island residents’ speech.
choices.C: the speech of the island’s residents revealed several shifts in the pronunciation of unstressed vowels to linguist Anika Vermeer.
choices.D: several shifts in the pronunciation of unstressed vowels were identified by linguist Anika Vermeer in the speech of the island’s residents.

questions.explanation: A is correct because the introductory participial phrase describes the person who compared the recordings and excluded equipment-related changes. Placing “linguist Anika Vermeer” immediately after that phrase gives it an appropriate subject to modify. D incorrectly attaches the introductory actions to “several shifts,” which cannot compare recordings. C attaches them to “the speech,” and B attaches them to “the pronunciation”; neither can perform the stated analytical actions. Mentioning Vermeer later in those choices does not repair the misplaced modifier.

questions.passage: When conservator Mateo Ibarra examined the tile fragment in 1972, he noticed a thin mineral deposit between its glaze and the clay beneath it. Later tests showed that the deposit _____ before the glaze was applied, so Ibarra’s original explanation—that it formed during decades of exposure in the museum courtyard—could not account for its location.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: will have developed
choices.B: is developing
choices.C: has developed
choices.D: had developed

questions.explanation: D is correct because the development of the deposit preceded another event in the past, the application of the glaze. The past perfect “had developed” clearly marks that earlier past event. B uses the present progressive and would place development in the present. A uses the future perfect and would place completion relative to a future point. C uses the present perfect, connecting past development to the present rather than locating it before the past application of the glaze.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Hester Lambert’s 1991 short story “The Quiet Shelf.” Tomas manages a workshop’s supplies.
No one asked Tomas why he counted the jars each evening. Their labels were clear; their contents scarcely changed from one day to the next. The shelves had not stood empty in a decade. Still, his fingers paused at each jar as if abundance were a promise that might be withdrawn before morning. The old fear took inventory long after the shortage itself had ended.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence “The shelves had not stood empty in a decade” in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It establishes that Tomas has recently improved a supply system that other workshop employees neglected.
choices.B: It suggests that Tomas’s daily counting has prevented a new shortage from occurring.
choices.C: It emphasizes the contrast between the workshop’s sustained material security and Tomas’s persistent anxiety.
choices.D: It reveals that the jars’ labels are inaccurate and therefore explains why Tomas must count them.

questions.explanation: C is correct because the long absence of empty shelves shows that supplies have been secure, making Tomas’s continued fearful counting striking. The later reference to an “old fear” clarifies that his anxiety outlasts its original cause. A introduces a recent improvement and other employees’ neglect, neither of which appears in the text. D contradicts the statement that the labels are clear and supplies scarcely change. B treats counting as the cause of adequate supplies, whereas the passage presents it as a lingering response to past insecurity.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Trees in central Malvera open their buds earlier than trees of the same species in the surrounding countryside. Because urban air is warmer, the city’s elevated temperature can account for this difference without requiring another explanation.
**Text 2**
Urban warmth can advance bud opening, but nighttime illumination may also matter. Researchers compared equally warm city streets where lamps were either left on or switched off overnight. Buds opened later on the unlit streets. The difference persisted even after the researchers accounted for small temperature variations among the streets.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the explanation because the urban and rural trees must have been different species
choices.B: By acknowledging that warmth can contribute while arguing that it does not fully explain the urban pattern
choices.C: By concluding that nighttime illumination is the only factor capable of affecting bud opening
choices.D: By arguing that the lighting comparison confirms that temperature alone determines when city trees open their buds

questions.explanation: B is correct because Text 2 explicitly accepts an effect of warmth but reports a lighting-related difference among similarly warm streets. That evidence challenges the sufficiency, rather than the existence, of temperature’s effect. A invents a species difference, while Text 1 specifies the same species. C overstates the finding and contradicts Text 2’s acknowledgment that warmth can matter. D reverses the implication of the comparison: a remaining difference associated with lighting counts against a temperature-only explanation.

questions.passage:
The following text is from Edda Rask’s 1938 poem “Noon Bell.”
Before the bell, I count the doors
As though their patient hinges kept the hours.
The bell arrives; the street is just the street,
Its unswept light still falling at my feet.
What freedom had I housed within that sound,
That, hearing it, I find I am still bound?
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The speaker regrets ignoring an earlier warning and resolves to obey the bell more closely in the future.
choices.B: The speaker finds that careful attention to ordinary objects makes the passing of time easier to endure.
choices.C: The speaker believes that other people misunderstand the bell’s practical purpose and wishes to correct them.
choices.D: The speaker anticipates freedom at a particular signal but discovers that the signal does not bring the expected release.

questions.explanation: D is correct because the speaker waits for the bell as though it promised freedom, then observes that the street remains unchanged and asks why the anticipated release has not occurred. “Still bound” expresses the continuing burden despite the signal. B assigns a comforting effect to counting the doors that the poem does not describe. A invents a warning, prior disobedience, and a future resolution. C shifts the focus to other people and the bell’s public function, neither of which the speaker discusses.

questions.passage: Researchers Amina Dossou and Leo Havel played the same tone to two groups of sandpipers across four training sessions. Each group heard ten tones per session over the same total period, but the tones arrived at regular intervals for one group and irregular intervals for the other. The researchers recorded how often the birds raised their heads in alertness. They suggest that habituation—the reduction of a response after repeated exposure—depends partly on temporal predictability, rather than on exposure count alone.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the researchers’ suggestion?

choices.A: The regular-interval group declined from eight to two responses, whereas the equally exposed irregular-interval group declined only to about six and a half.
choices.B: The irregular-interval group declined from eight to about six and a half responses, showing that alert responses disappeared regardless of timing.
choices.C: The regular-interval group averaged fewer responses in the fourth session, demonstrating that the groups differed before training began.
choices.D: Both of the groups averaged eight alert responses in the first session, indicating that predictability could have had no effect in later sessions.

questions.explanation: A is correct because the response decreases much more under regular timing even though exposure count and total session duration are matched. That difference is consistent with a contribution of predictability to habituation. D incorrectly assumes that equal initial responses prevent the groups from responding differently as training proceeds. B turns a modest decline into complete disappearance; approximately 6.5 responses remain. C reports a final difference but wrongly uses it to infer a difference before training.

graph.caption: Alert responses across four training sessions

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
Marceau Lenoir’s 1762 travel account *Across the Vara Plateau* survives in two later handwritten copies.
Both copies misspell the town name Rivala as Rilava.
Historian Emil Ishikawa argues that the shared error proves the copies were made from the same intermediate manuscript.
Elias Thorn’s 1757 regional atlas also uses the spelling Rilava.
Both copyists had access to Thorn’s atlas.
questions.question: The student wants to explain why the shared error alone does not establish that the copies descended from the same intermediate manuscript. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Because each copyist could have borrowed the spelling Rilava from Thorn’s atlas, the shared error need not have originated in a common intermediate manuscript.
choices.B: Thorn’s atlas appeared before Lenoir’s account and was available to both later copyists.
choices.C: Ishikawa bases his argument for a common intermediate manuscript on the fact that both copies use Rilava rather than Rivala.
choices.D: The copies cannot share an intermediate manuscript because their copyists both had access to a regional atlas.

questions.explanation: A is correct because it uses the atlas as a specific alternative source of the error, directly explaining why the shared spelling is insufficient proof of a common intermediate copy. D goes too far: access to the atlas does not rule out a shared manuscript; it merely makes another explanation possible. C summarizes the argument being challenged without addressing its limitation. B supplies relevant background but leaves unstated how that background weakens the inference about the copies’ ancestry.

questions.passage: Uncorrected scans of the Karlen charts sometimes make straight grid lines appear curved, a distortion that could be mistaken for a feature of the original cartographer’s technique. _____ map researcher Hector Nyambe calibrated the scanning system against sheets with known straight-line patterns before measuring the charts’ geometry.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Accordingly,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: Likewise,
choices.D: On the contrary,

questions.explanation: A is correct because the calibration is a response to the identified risk: a known reference lets Nyambe account for scanner distortion before attributing geometry to the original charts. D would signal that the second sentence contradicts the first, but the procedure addresses the problem rather than denying it. C would imply a similar preceding action, while the first sentence describes a risk, not a calibration action. B would present Nyambe’s procedure as an example of the distortion, although it is a measure taken to control that distortion.

questions.passage: After examining the surviving fragments of a folded ceremonial banner, curator Adelina Pereira identified three features that any proposed reconstruction would need to _____ the direction of the woven fibers, the overlap of the joins, and the placement of the suspension holes.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: preserve;
choices.B: preserve:
choices.C: preserve.
choices.D: preserve

questions.explanation: B is correct because the complete clause before the colon announces “three features,” and the list after the colon specifies those features. C uses a period, leaving the following noun list as an incomplete sentence. A uses a semicolon, but the material after it is a noun list rather than an independent clause. D leaves the introductory clause and its explanatory list unseparated, producing an improperly joined sequence.

questions.passage: Botanist Nuria Esquivel sought to trace how knowledge of coastal plants spread. Specimens collected by Samuel Kline, _____ were central to her comparison of two independently compiled herbals.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: an itinerant surveyor who worked near Vardona in the 1860s:
choices.B: an itinerant surveyor who worked near Vardona in the 1860s
choices.C: an itinerant surveyor who worked near Vardona in the 1860s;
choices.D: an itinerant surveyor who worked near Vardona in the 1860s,

questions.explanation: D is correct because the description of Samuel Kline is a nonessential appositive. The comma already supplied before it must be matched by a comma after it, allowing the main construction “Specimens ... were central” to resume. B leaves the appositive without its required closing comma. C and A substitute a semicolon or colon for that comma; neither appropriately closes the inserted description or connects it to the main predicate “were central.”

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Danelia Voss’s 1927 novel *The Ninth Window*. Mina has been waiting for visitors who may offer her a commission.
When they entered, Mina did not rise at once. She let her gaze remain on the open ledger, turned a page that she had already read, and only then looked up. Her indifference was studied: she had rehearsed these small delays all morning, hoping to appear less dependent on their decision than she felt.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does “studied” most nearly mean?

choices.A: Uncertain
choices.B: Detailed
choices.C: Informed
choices.D: Deliberate

questions.explanation: D is correct because Mina consciously plans and rehearses the appearance of indifference. The delayed gestures are calculated rather than spontaneous. C would describe a judgment based on knowledge, but the word modifies her manner, not her understanding of the visitors. B would emphasize completeness or specificity, which is not the relevant sense. A conflicts with her purposeful rehearsal; although she is anxious about the decision, her outward behavior is intentionally arranged.

questions.passage: Long silences in performances of Renaud Cho’s chamber piece are often interpreted as moments of improvised hesitation. Musicologist Ava Cornejo found that early performance parts assign exact bar counts to many of those silences. The markings do not mean that every performance should sound identical, she argues, but they show that the interruptions cannot all be attributed to spontaneous decisions by performers.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It proposes a new performance practice, gives instructions for implementing it, and predicts how audiences will respond.
choices.B: It describes a musicologist’s methods and establishes that the methods recover the composer’s complete intentions with certainty.
choices.C: It identifies a common interpretation, presents documentary evidence that challenges it, and states a qualified conclusion drawn from that evidence.
choices.D: It compares two interpretations of a musical work and concludes that neither can be evaluated without recordings.

questions.explanation: C is correct because the text moves from the usual account of the silences as improvisation to written bar counts that challenge that account, then limits the conclusion to saying that not all interruptions are spontaneous. A invents a proposed practice and audience prediction. D incorrectly says the interpretations cannot be evaluated; the performance parts provide relevant evidence. B exaggerates the conclusion into complete recovery of the composer’s intentions, whereas Cornejo explicitly allows variation among performances.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from Sada Moriyama’s 1987 novel *The Last Awning*. Riko repairs fabric awnings.
The customer congratulated Riko on matching the pattern so perfectly. She accepted the compliment, folded the awning, and placed it beside the door. After he had gone, however, she opened it again and removed four stitches. No one standing in the street would notice the small misalignment they held in place. Riko noticed it; under the afternoon light, that was sufficient.
questions.question: Which inference about Riko is most strongly supported by the text?

choices.A: She suspects that the customer’s praise was intended to pressure her into lowering her price.
choices.B: She expects that passersby will complain about the awning unless the customer examines it more carefully.
choices.C: Her judgment of satisfactory work can be more demanding than the judgment of a pleased customer.
choices.D: She regrets accepting the repair because the original pattern is impossible to reproduce accurately.

questions.explanation: C is correct because Riko reopens an item that the customer praised and corrects a flaw that others would not notice. Her own recognition of the flaw is enough to motivate additional work. A assigns an unstated financial motive to the customer. D overstates a small misalignment as an impossible repair and introduces regret absent from the passage. B contradicts the statement that people in the street would not notice the flaw.

questions.passage: “The Reopened Gate” is a 1952 poem by Celine Hartung. In the poem, the speaker values the restoration of an old garden while recognizing that restoring its appearance cannot fully recover the past.
questions.question: Which quotation from “The Reopened Gate” most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.A: “Across the loosened soil the young shoots rise; / their green makes even the noon’s sharp glare / a gentler thing to bear.”
choices.B: “Leave every broken trellis where it falls; / no hand should set the branches back in line / or ask the closed gate to receive us.”
choices.C: “The gate leaned inward through the winter rain; / whoever left it there has let the seasons / settle what a keeper should have mended.”
choices.D: “I bless the paths that find their stones again; / yet no restored rose calls the vanished hands / that taught it once to climb.”

questions.explanation: D is correct because “bless” expresses appreciation for the recovered paths while the reference to “vanished hands” states that restoration cannot bring back the people associated with the earlier garden. C criticizes neglect without expressing the speaker’s qualified appreciation of restoration. A praises new growth but does not acknowledge the unrecoverable past. B rejects restoration altogether, which conflicts with the claim that the speaker values it.

questions.passage:
**Spellings in Dated Manuscripts**
In 1170, the Council of Senavra prescribed the spelling Velora for a region previously written as Vellora. Historian Dario Kessler classified the spelling used in surviving manuscripts copied during three periods. He argues that, in the latest period sampled, the prescribed form had become predominant without completely displacing the older form.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Kessler’s argument?

choices.A: All forty manuscripts sampled from 1140–1169 use the older spelling.
choices.B: Sixty manuscripts were sampled from 1200–1229, compared with fifty from 1170–1199.
choices.C: Among manuscripts sampled from 1200–1229, 75% use the prescribed spelling, but 25% still use the older spelling.
choices.D: Among manuscripts sampled from 1170–1199, 54% use the older spelling and 46% use the prescribed spelling.

questions.explanation: C is correct because the prescribed spelling appears in a majority of the latest manuscripts while a substantial minority still use the older form. The two percentages establish both parts of Kessler’s argument: predominance and incomplete replacement. A concerns the period before the prescription and cannot demonstrate the later result. D concerns the middle period, when the prescribed form was not yet predominant, rather than the latest period named in the claim. B reports sample sizes, which do not indicate which spelling was used.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
Researcher Eleni Markou investigated a carved figure made by Celia Mantovani in 1874.
Tomographic scans revealed how wooden sections were joined beneath the figure’s exterior covering.
Chemical tests identified ingredients in the finish applied to the figure’s surface.
The scans supplied information about internal assembly.
The chemical tests supplied information about the materials in the exterior finish.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how the two methods contributed different kinds of information to Markou’s investigation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Markou combined scans that revealed the figure’s internal assembly with chemical tests that identified materials in its surface finish.
choices.B: By identifying the finish’s ingredients, the scans showed Markou how the wooden sections were joined.
choices.C: Chemical tests identified ingredients in the finish on a carved figure whose wooden sections lay beneath an exterior covering.
choices.D: Markou used both tomographic scans and chemical tests to investigate Mantovani’s 1874 carved figure.

questions.explanation: A is correct because it explicitly assigns a distinct contribution to each method: structural information from scans and material information from chemical tests. D names the methods and their shared subject but omits their different contributions. B incorrectly attributes the chemical tests’ result to the scans and treats that result as evidence about the joints. C describes the chemical tests and the object, but it does not explain what the scans contributed.

questions.passage: Three curators kept separate records of the same collection, and each recorded a different judgment about the origin of its oldest carved panel. Although the panel itself has changed little, the _____ preserve a sequence of changing attributions.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: curators’ record
choices.B: curators’ records
choices.C: curators record’s
choices.D: curator’s records’

questions.explanation: B is correct because the records belong to multiple curators, requiring the plural possessive “curators’,” and the plural noun “records” agrees with “preserve.” C fails to mark the curators as possessors and instead incorrectly makes “record” possessive. D makes both the possessor and the record noun possessive, leaving no appropriate nonpossessive head noun for the subject. A correctly marks multiple curators as possessors but uses the singular “record,” which does not agree with the plural verb “preserve.”

questions.passage: Textile scholar Natalia Roven’s first catalog—an attempt to classify stitched patterns without relying on their local names_____ its later supplement remain useful sources despite disagreements about her categories.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: and
choices.B: ; and
choices.C: , and
choices.D: —and

questions.explanation: D is correct because the second em dash closes the nonessential description that begins after “catalog.” The remaining sentence has the compound subject “Roven’s first catalog ... and its later supplement,” which agrees with “remain.” C incorrectly pairs the opening em dash with a comma. B does not close the inserted description and uses a semicolon where the compound subject must continue. A omits the closing punctuation, leaving the description improperly joined to the rest of the subject.

questions.passage: To investigate an apparent change in ink shading, bibliographer Davi Serrano distinguishes copies _____ from copies made after the publisher replaced the worn printing plate.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: , that were printed from the first plate,
choices.B: that were printed from the first plate,
choices.C: that were printed from the first plate
choices.D: , that were printed from the first plate

questions.explanation: C is correct because the relative clause identifies which copies Serrano distinguishes from the later copies. It is essential to that distinction and therefore should not be set off by commas. B adds an unnecessary comma between the first category and the “from” phrase that completes the comparison. A places commas around an identifying clause and incorrectly treats it as nonessential. D likewise introduces the identifying clause with an inappropriate comma and does not properly close the resulting insertion.

questions.passage: Curator Renata Maier sent an unsigned print to two scholars _____ she believed could identify its maker from the combination of its paper fibers and engraved borders.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: who
choices.B: whom
choices.C: which
choices.D: whose

questions.explanation: A is correct because the relative pronoun serves as the subject of “could identify”: the scholars could identify the maker. The intervening words “she believed” do not change that subject role. B uses the object form “whom,” even though the blank is not the object of the earlier preposition “to” or of “believed.” D is possessive and cannot serve as the required subject. C ordinarily refers to things rather than the people identified here as scholars.

questions.passage:
**Text 1**
Several early botanical catalogs surround each illustration with the same ornamental frame. Because a repeated frame conveys no information specific to the plant inside it, these borders should be understood as purely decorative additions, with no practical role in the catalogs.
**Text 2**
A visual element need not distinguish one plant from another to assist a reader. In tests using reproductions of the catalogs, readers located the associated descriptive passages more quickly when the familiar frames remained visible than when the frames were removed. The borders evidently helped readers orient themselves on the page.
questions.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?

choices.A: By disputing the assumption that a visual feature must convey plant-specific information to perform a practical function
choices.B: By denying that any of the catalogs used the same frame around more than one illustration
choices.C: By accepting that a frame cannot have a practical role unless it identifies the species depicted inside it
choices.D: By claiming that every ornamental border necessarily improves the accuracy of plant identification

questions.explanation: A is correct because Text 2 supplies a practical function—helping readers locate associated information—that does not require a frame to identify a particular plant. This directly challenges the premise connecting lack of plant-specific information with purely decorative status. C repeats the premise Text 2 rejects. D extends the finding to every border and to identification accuracy, neither of which the tests establish. B contradicts the shared premise that the catalogs contain repeated frames rather than addressing what those frames do.

questions.passage: Human-factors researcher Salma Okafor tested how letter spacing affects the transcription of small printed labels. Participants read labels with either standard or widened spacing under diffuse light and under strong glare. Each condition involved one hundred labels, and the vocabulary and type size were held constant. Okafor argues that widening the spacing helped more under glare than under diffuse light.
questions.question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Okafor’s argument?

choices.A: With standard spacing, the mean fell from 86 correct labels under diffuse light to 52 under glare.
choices.B: Widened spacing increased the mean by 26 correct labels under glare but by only 2 under diffuse light.
choices.C: Widened spacing raised the glare-condition mean from 52 to 78 correct labels, completely eliminating the disadvantage of glare.
choices.D: Under diffuse light, participants transcribed 88 labels correctly with widened spacing and 86 with standard spacing.

questions.explanation: B is correct because it compares the effect of spacing within each lighting condition: 78 minus 52 is 26, whereas 88 minus 86 is 2. The larger gain under glare directly supports Okafor’s claim. C overstates the improvement; the glare mean with widened spacing remains below the diffuse-light mean with widened spacing. D establishes a small spacing benefit in diffuse light but does not compare that benefit with the glare benefit. A shows an effect of lighting with standard spacing, not the difference between the two spacing effects.

questions.passage: Indexing every spoken phrase in the Oren Oral History Archive would require many times more staff hours than indexing interviews only by speaker and date. _____ curator Zanele Mbeki chose phrase-level indexing because it would allow researchers to locate a brief reference to an event even when they did not know which interview contained it.
questions.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For instance,
choices.B: Nevertheless,
choices.C: Consequently,
choices.D: Similarly,

questions.explanation: B is correct because Mbeki chooses the more labor-intensive approach despite the drawback identified in the first sentence. The second sentence supplies the benefit that motivates her choice. C would present choosing that approach as a direct consequence of its greater labor requirement, although the passage gives a separate benefit as the reason. D would require a preceding comparable decision rather than a contrast between cost and choice. A would introduce an example of the greater staff-hour requirement, but the second sentence describes a decision and its research benefit.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
Engineer Ansel Rojas proposed a lightweight bridge design in 1894.
Rojas estimated resistance to wind using measurements from static-load tests.
Reviewer Nalin Pradhan criticized that estimate because static-load measurements did not establish how the design would behave in changing winds.
Pradhan supported the use of lightweight materials when their behavior had been adequately tested.
Pradhan’s review did not reject lightweight bridge construction in general.
questions.question: The student wants to distinguish Pradhan’s specific criticism from a general objection to lightweight construction. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Although Pradhan supported adequately tested lightweight materials, he objected to Rojas’s use of static-load measurements to estimate the bridge’s behavior in changing winds.
choices.B: Pradhan reviewed Rojas’s bridge proposal and questioned an estimate included in its supporting analysis.
choices.C: Pradhan’s criticism of the 1894 proposal demonstrates that he opposed lightweight materials in bridge construction.
choices.D: Rojas proposed a lightweight bridge and estimated its resistance to wind from measurements collected in static-load tests.

questions.explanation: A is correct because it explicitly contrasts Pradhan’s support for tested lightweight materials with his objection to one unsupported method of estimating wind behavior. That distinction accomplishes the student’s goal. C contradicts the notes by turning a specific criticism into general opposition. D summarizes Rojas’s method without describing Pradhan’s position. B mentions the criticism but does not distinguish it from an objection to lightweight construction more broadly.
